raw_text:
**Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Concise Narrative Review**

### Introduction and Epidemiology
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a life-threatening, pregnancy-associated myocardial disease characterized by idiopathic left ventricular (LV) dysfunction and heart failure [1]. Traditionally, diagnostic criteria required heart failure onset in the last month of pregnancy or within five months postpartum [2,3]. However, modern consensus definitions extend this clinical window to any peripartum state, necessitating the exclusion of other identifiable causes of heart failure and a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) typically below 45% [4,5].

The global epidemiology of PPCM reveals significant regional variation [6]. In the United States, the incidence is estimated between 1 in 1,000 and 1 in 4,000 live births [5], whereas much higher rates are documented in regions like Haiti (1 in 300) and parts of Africa [6,8]. Recent registry and population studies confirm a rising global incidence [7,9]. Key risk factors include advanced maternal age, African ancestry, multi-fetal gestations, and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, particularly preeclampsia, which shares a close pathophysiological connection with PPCM [10].

### Pathophysiology
The current understanding of PPCM is driven by a "two-hit" hypothesis involving a systemic vascular insult combined with a genetic predisposition. The peripartum period is marked by high oxidative stress, which triggers the cleavage of the hormone prolactin by cathepsin D into a cardiotoxic 16-kDa N-terminal fragment [11]. This fragment is highly anti-angiogenic, pro-apoptotic, and pro-inflammatory, inducing endothelial damage and capillary dissociation [11,12]. This process is exacerbated by placental secretion of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt1), which neutralizes vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) [12]. Additionally, the 16-kDa fragment stimulates the release of microRNA-146a-loaded exosomes from endothelial cells, promoting cardiomyocyte apoptosis [13].

Genetically, PPCM overlaps significantly with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) [14]. Approximately 10% to 15% of PPCM patients carry truncating mutations in sarcomeric genes, most commonly the titin gene (*TTN*) [15]. Autoimmune mechanisms also contribute, as evidenced by autoantibodies against cardiac troponin I and sarcomeric myosin [16].

### Diagnosis and Management
Early diagnosis is challenging because normal physiological symptoms of late pregnancy overlap with those of early heart failure [17]. Echocardiography remains the gold standard for confirming systolic dysfunction, and elevated N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) serves as a sensitive biomarker [17].

Management strategies are tailored according to pre- or postpartum presentation [18]. Prior to delivery, standard heart failure therapies such as angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEis), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs), and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) are contraindicated due to fetotoxicity [17,18]. Instead, afterload reduction is achieved using hydralazine and nitrates, while beta-blockers and diuretics are carefully managed [18]. In severe cardiogenic shock, mechanical circulatory support may be required to unload the left ventricle [19]. Due to the high risk of life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias, a wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (WCD) is recommended in the acute phase of severely reduced LVEF [20].

### Specific Therapies and Recovery
Based on the prolactin cleavage pathway, the dopamine D2 receptor agonist bromocriptine has emerged as a disease-specific treatment [21]. Bromocriptine blocks pituitary prolactin release, preventing the generation of the toxic 16-kDa fragment. A multicenter randomized trial demonstrated that adding bromocriptine to standard heart failure treatment is associated with high rates of LV recovery and low morbidity [22]. Concomitant therapeutic anticoagulation is mandatory to mitigate the high thromboembolic risk associated with PPCM and lactation suppression [23].

Fortunately, PPCM has a higher rate of myocardial recovery than other cardiomyopathies [24]. Approximately 50% to 70% of patients recover normal LV function (LVEF $\ge$ 50%) [24,25]. The "ESC EORP PPCM Recovery Score" has been developed to help clinicians estimate this probability [25]. However, some patients suffer from persistent cardiac dysfunction, late declines in ejection fraction, or significant chronic cardiovascular comorbidities [9,26].

### Subsequent Pregnancies and Prognosis
Subsequent pregnancies carry a substantial risk of relapse, particularly in women with persistent LV dysfunction [27,28]. Pre-conception counseling is vital; if LVEF has not fully recovered, subsequent pregnancy is highly discouraged due to maternal mortality rates approaching 20% [27,28]. For those with normalized function, subsequent pregnancy still carries a relapse risk of up to 20%, requiring close monitoring by a multidisciplinary cardio-obstetrics team [28-30].
